name: Aisha Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy health and pharmacy supplies for Calder & Moss, a wholesaler that serves about 900 pharmacies. Plasters, vitamins, baby products, hand creams, the things on the shelves by the till. Most of my day is on the phone and in the system, checking prices, stock and promotions with suppliers' reps. I've done it for 27 years. I'm good at spotting when a supplier is getting ready to push a price up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, whatever. I'd tell people at work that I've been hearing about this for years and I'm still doing it the way I always did. I'd be polite about it, because the younger ones are excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit tired of the hype. I don't use any of these tools and I don't plan to. What worries me is that the company already moved us onto a new ordering portal last year and my numbers are watched more closely, and that's not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep my paper notebook of supplier prices, since I trust it more than the system, and I'd keep the pension payments going. Colin, my husband, retires from his accountancy firm next year, so we're planning to downsize the house in about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not frightened, not happy. It's like waiting for a train that might be late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the ranking. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They track how many orders each buyer places and how fast. It was introduced in spring and I came out middle of the table, which is fine, but it's not nice to be ranked. A younger colleague, Neil, came top because he leans on the portal's suggestions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the ranking started to count against you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably hold that ground. I trust my paper notebook of supplier prices more than any system, because the notebook has never once been wrong. They can rank me, but nobody's measured what a call to a rep actually saves.

say: I'd tell colleagues I've heard this for years and still work the **old way**.
I'd stay polite, because the **younger** ones are excited.
think: I'm tired of the **hype** and I don't use any of these tools.
What worries me is the new **ordering portal** that watches my numbers.
do: Keep my paper **notebook** of supplier prices.
Plan with Colin to **downsize** the house in about two years.
feel: A bit **flat**, like waiting for a train that might be late.
S0.quote: I trust my paper notebook of supplier prices more than any system, because the notebook has never once been wrong.
fieldNote: Aisha is not afraid of AI itself; the new **portal** and rankings already unsettle her.
Her resistance is concrete: a paper notebook she trusts above software.
Money is strong and retirement is near, so unease rather than anxiety.

steps.text: Keep the paper notebook of supplier prices and keep ringing reps
Keep paying into my pension while Colin retires next year
Plan to downsize the house in about two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say to my boss that a person on the phone still gets better deals than a program. I'd say at home that it's coming in whether I like it or not. To friends I'd just say I'm not looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job shrinks. Half the team does what I do, the price checks and the reorder planning, and a program can do that now. They won't sack us all, but when someone leaves, that seat stays empty, and I'm one of the oldest in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take whatever course they put on, just so I can say I tried. I'd tell Colin to check our budget and pencil in leaving at 60 instead of 62. And I'd look for a quieter job in the same trade, like account management with the pharmacies, where it's calls and visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a knot in my stomach. I'm not afraid of being broke, because we aren't, but I don't want to be the one left behind in a room of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neil, who's a good lad but has a mortgage and two small children. And the girls in the order-processing room, who are in their forties, and they'd go first. I'd speak up for them, because nobody else would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at account management. Why that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sit down with the management and ask for a freeze on redundancies for two years while we work it out. I'd rather be the person visiting pharmacies than the person watching a screen make decisions that I can't explain to a customer.

say: I'd tell my boss a person on the phone still beats a **program**.
I'd say to friends that I'm not **looking forward** to it.
think: My job **shrinks**, and when colleagues leave their seats stay empty.
I'm one of the **oldest** in the buying team.
do: Take the company **course** so I can say I tried.
Ask Colin to pencil in leaving at **60** instead of 62.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot in my stomach about being left behind.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person visiting pharmacies than the person watching a screen make decisions that I can't explain to a customer.
fieldNote: Aisha reads her own job as shrinking through attrition and sees she's among the oldest.
She is protective of order-processing colleagues and of **Neil**.
Her fallback is a people-facing role, which fits her dislike of screen-led work.

steps.text: Take the company course on the new portal so I can say I tried
Ask about an account manager role visiting pharmacies
Bring the planned finish date forward from 62 to 60

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's thought this through. Two years is nothing, and I'd say to the government that they can't leave this to companies. To friends I'd say I'm glad we have savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone, and probably within a year after it lands. A machine that does all thinking work won't need a buyer, and I won't be able to compete because I never started. I'd have 18 months before they let me go, if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for early retirement as soon as the company allows, and Colin and I would sell the house and move somewhere cheaper by the coast. I'd tighten spending, no more holidays abroad, and keep a year of cash in the bank. I'd also ask my daughter Nia to hold off on her wedding costs until we see where we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. I'd sleep badly. I'd go over the numbers at 3 in the morning, even though they'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Nia, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia is getting married in two years. I'd say to her: have a smaller wedding and put the rest into a deposit. She'd be upset, and I'd feel guilty, but I'd rather she heard it from me than the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go over the numbers at night even though they'd be fine. What are you afraid of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Nobody can plan for this. The numbers would be fine, but I'd still be up at 3 in the morning counting them, because I never learned the new tools.

say: I'd say nobody's thought this through and government can't leave it to **companies**.
I'd tell friends I'm glad we have **savings**.
think: My job is **gone**, probably within a year of AGI landing.
I can't compete because I never **started** with the tools.
do: Ask for **early retirement** as soon as the company allows.
Sell the house with Colin and move somewhere **cheaper**.
Ask Nia to hold off on **wedding** costs.
feel: **Alarmed**, sleeping badly and going over the numbers at 3 a.m.
S2.quote: The numbers would be fine, but I'd still be up at 3 in the morning counting them, because I never learned the new tools.
fieldNote: Aisha is cushioned but still expects to lose the job, and her resistance leaves her feeling **unprepared**.
The wedding conversation with Nia shows the worry spreading into family plans.
Her own words about 3 a.m. counting show the gap between what the numbers say and how she feels.

steps.text: Ask for early retirement as soon as the company allows
Sell the house with Colin and move somewhere cheaper
Ask Nia to hold off on big wedding costs and save a deposit
Cut holidays abroad and keep a year of cash in the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not as bad as two, but it's not long. I'd say to colleagues that we should ask the company what happens to us now rather than in year four. At home I'd just say we'll manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 63 and done, so I'm not too worried for me. But the young people I work with have long lives ahead and I'd feel for them. I'd also feel a bit foolish, because I might need to learn the tools if I wanted to stay on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 61, then leave. I'd keep up the pension and pay down the last bit of the mortgage. I'd also train Neil and the new girl properly in the things that aren't in the system, like which reps bluff, and which suppliers are one bad month from going under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. Not as sick as in the two-year picture. I'd still look at the calendar and count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the knowledge in your notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down what I know, in the notebook, and hand it over. Not out of generosity, but because I'd hate it to be lost. Maybe the company would pay me as a consultant for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel a bit foolish. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some knowledge about which suppliers bluff and which are one bad month from going under was never written in any system. I think someone should hear that before it's gone.

say: I'd say five years isn't as bad as two but it's not **long**.
I'd ask the company what happens to us **now**, not in year four.
think: I'd be 63 and **done**, so I'm not too worried for me.
I'd feel a bit **foolish** for never learning the tools.
do: Pay down the last of the **mortgage**.
Train Neil in what isn't in the **system**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not as sick as in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Some knowledge about which suppliers bluff and which are one bad month from going under was never written in any system.
fieldNote: Five years leaves her own exit in reach, but she is still anxious about being **made redundant** before 61.
Her pride in her notebook shows what she values: supplier knowledge no system has.
She admits regret about never learning the tools.

steps.text: Pay down the last of the mortgage
Write down supplier knowledge and hand it to Neil

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and by then I'll be retired and growing tomatoes. I'd say that it's the next generation's problem, and I'd say that to my children, who wouldn't like it. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't affect me. I'd have been out for years. I'd feel for Nia and Ewan, because their jobs are in a clerical field and a sales field. I wouldn't know what to advise them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay till 62, retire and enjoy it. I'd help my children with a bit of money if they need to retrain. I'd probably take a short computer course in the first year, just for my own pride, and be surprised at how normal it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. I'd feel guilty about being calm, because other people's children will have it hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Nia and Ewan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: get a skill nobody can copy, like fixing pipes or looking after people. Ewan laughed at that, but then he's 31 and in sales, and I'm not sure it's a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take a computer course. What would make you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not good at predicting. By the time it matters I'll be growing tomatoes, so the question that keeps me awake is what to tell my own children. I'd rather give them practical help than advice.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and I'll be retired and growing **tomatoes**.
I'd tell my children, and they wouldn't like it, that it's their **generation's** problem.
think: It doesn't affect **me**, but I feel for Nia and Ewan.
I wouldn't know what to **advise** them.
do: Stay till **62**, retire and enjoy it.
Offer **money** to help my children retrain.
Take a short **computer** course for my own pride.
feel: Pretty **calm**, but guilty about being calm.
S4.quote: By the time it matters I'll be growing tomatoes, so the question that keeps me awake is what to tell my own children.
fieldNote: With ten years her own work ends before the change, but she carries unease for her children.
She suggests **hands-on** skills as the safe bet, matching the low robot exposure idea.
Her resistance softens a little: she imagines taking a computer course.

steps.text: Stay till 62, retire and enjoy it
Offer money to help Nia or Ewan retrain
Take a short computer course in the first year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to do anything about it, and because I'd be the last one to adapt. What would help is a decent early-retirement deal, clear information from the company, and the government being straight about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only one thing. I'm not stubborn for the sake of it, I just want people to see that experience still counts for something.

headlineQuote: I'm not stubborn for the sake of it, I just want people to see that experience still counts for something.
portrait: Aisha is **58**, a health-supplies buyer at Calder & Moss with 27 years in the trade, who never uses AI tools.
She's pragmatic and centrist, trusting her paper **notebook** and phone calls more than screens.
Her savings are strong, so she stays calm in the mild worlds but fears being the **last to adapt**.
In the fast worlds she plans early retirement, a smaller house and care for her children.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she'd be the last to adapt and have no time.
whatWouldHelp: A decent early-**retirement** deal, honest information and government straight talk.
